draft.title: News report structure
card: Headline
a short title that names the story. It is often in the present tense, such as "Fire closes town library".
Lead
the first paragraph. It gives the most important facts and answers who, what, when, where, why and how.
Body
the paragraphs after the lead. They add detail, such as quotes and background, with the most important detail first and the least important last.
This is called the inverted pyramid. A reader who stops after the lead still knows the main story, and an editor can cut the last paragraphs without losing the main facts.
draft.remember: Put the main facts first, then add detail from most to least important.

a.q: Why does a news report put the main facts in the first paragraph?
opts: A reader who stops early still gets the main story
It lets the writer give their opinion on the event
It makes the story follow the order events happened
It lets the report build up suspense for the reader
a.why: The lead holds the most important facts, so a reader who stops early still knows what happened. Telling events in time order is a different structure, and it can bury the main facts near the end.
a.clue: Think about a reader who only has time for one paragraph.

b.q: Priya is writing a report on a flooded school oval in Bendigo. Which sentence belongs in her lead?
opts: Heavy rain flooded the school oval on Monday morning
The oval was built in 1962 and is often used for sport
The principal said the clean-up would take most of a week
Students got a free day while workers pumped out water
b.why: The first sentence answers what, where and when, so it is the main fact of the story. The other three are detail that suits the body: background, a quote and a smaller result. The quote is tempting, but a quote adds detail and does not state the main event.
b.clue: Which sentence tells the reader what happened, where and when?

a.best: A reader who stops early still gets the main story

b.best: Heavy rain flooded the school oval on Monday morning
